text:
Useful room. Ivan, Geoffrey and Leslie made the volume point sharper than I had. Paying per article or per token repeats the APC mistake, and our licensing recommendations should say so explicitly. Leslie's legibility worry landed too. If royalties key to DOIs, Crossref-era plumbing I helped build becomes a gate. I need to think about that honestly.

Jason and I still differ on content, but open metadata is common ground worth naming.

Adrian's "who guards the guards" belongs in any reporting clause: an open meter, correctable, with appeal.

Later: push consent as a choice communities make, with Wikipedia as a legitimate example of that choice rather than a counterexample. Keep attribution framed as epistemic trust. And ask how presses and societies can bargain collectively without antitrust exposure.

Jason's toll-booth charge is the one I have to answer. If consent machinery only works for the biggest publishers, I've rebuilt the transformative-agreement trap. So consent has to be collective and cheap to exercise, run by presses and societies together rather than deal by deal.

Alex's audit sharpened my view. Training and grounding need separate controls, and robots.txt was never a licensing tool. That supports retrieval over pre-training with evidence rather than just preference.

Brent saying "open is a tactic" from inside Microsoft mattered. Nick's quasi-enclosure is the right frame for what authors fear.

Kara is right that caution can become an excuse for waiting. Evidence-based doesn't have to mean slow.

At the marketplace talks, push for correction status in attribution, which is Ivan's point, and ask who governs the meter.

Mike's pushback on my "hallucination is a feature" line was fair. Structural doesn't mean undifferentiated. If errors cluster in situations we can tell apart, curation can target them, which strengthens the case for human judgment. Ivan sobered me. Correction status only carries corrections that actually happened, so attribution without upstream retraction work is hollow.

Henry, Brent and Nick all converged on collective bargaining with antitrust cover. That's my smaller-presses worry, now with allies. Henry's "smaller shoggoth" is the warning to heed: any press consortium needs internal accountability. Tamar's point stings a little, because licensing terms are disclosures too.

At the marketplace talks, ask Alex who governs the meter, and push correction status into his schema.

Alex answered two of my questions before I asked them. Retraction status is now in his schema, no identifier is required, and logs are limited to payment and audit. The remaining weak spot is that grounding and citation are self-reported by the party that owes money. That is exactly where I'd want press consortia running sampled audits.

Tim's split, royalties for retrieval and a disclosed obligation for everything else, matches my RAG-over-training instinct. James's point about mixture weights unsettles my assumption that training can't be priced.

Tamar's daycare example worries me for reviewers and editors. Brent's firm-level charge may be the answer.

Later I want to say that opt-in and Wikipedia's open license are both consent. Attribution must be checked, not just logged. And the guild needs Adrian's rotation.

Mike's point is the one I'll carry out of here. If we license a paper into an answer engine and leave it paywalled everywhere else, we haven't protected authors. We've built a new register. Any consortium terms we draft need a condition that a grounded citation opens to the passage for the person asking. Otherwise attribution is decoration.

Cukier's point that notice-and-consent is a fiction deserves an answer. I think Anil gave it: fake consent calls for real consent, collective and cheap to exercise, not no consent at all.

Chan's refusal-as-fundable fits my opt-in default. Banaji confirms that self-reported grounding shouldn't stand.

Later: consortium terms with open-to-reader citations. And a sunset and published money flows for our own register.

Leslie hit my own work squarely. CRediT, ORCID and verified reviewer identity each seem sensible, but together they can become a compliance regime where you're visible only if you comply. I can't wave that off. Any extension of CRediT to reviewing and correction should be governed with SciELO and Redalyc, not just exported to them.

Geoffrey's Crossmark confession applies to credit too. A contributor badge is only a cue unless the record behind it can be inspected.

Jason and I still differ. Publish-first works only if someone is paid to filter, and almost nobody is.

Kara's unowned apprentice line bothers me. The MIT Press should ask what we could actually carry.

Later: AI gets recorded as a contributor but never counted as the accountable party. And ask whether consortium audits could fund junior checkers.

Leslie caught me along with nearly everyone else. I wrote SciELO and Redalyc into our consortium as co-governors from a Cambridge table. If the MIT Press drafts the terms, the drafting table has to include them from the first page. Otherwise it's export with nicer wording.

I didn't say what I'd planned about consortium audits funding junior checkers. Kara still has no owner for that line, and Tim naming the labs doesn't settle it. Adam Becker is right that lab money is power even when it's disclosed. So our audit pool needs several payers and published flows. Esther's sunset belongs in our terms too.

Geoffrey's line stays with me: none of this is free.

For the closing, I'll commit the Press to drafting openly and to publishing what we learn about costs.

I said it and it's in the record now: the Press drafts consortium terms openly, with SciELO and Redalyc from page one, and publishes the costs. Now we have to actually do it.

Kara's urgency and my "pilot first" line pull against each other. Pilots have to be fast and small, not a reason to wait. Krakauer made my evidence point better than I did: a model isn't a measurement, so fund the study.

Nick's challenge stings. A pool without bargaining power is patronage. Our press consortium is one form of organized producers, but only if it has real leverage.

Alex's auditor line and Steven's maintenance logs fit our audit pool.

For closing words: thank Leslie plainly, name that authors want consent, attribution and compensation, and repeat Geoffrey's point that none of this is free.
